15009.q: What is the distribution of seats in the Federal Council that applied from 1959 called?
15009.e: From 1959 the FDP, CVP and SP each got two seats and the SVP one seat. In 2003 one CVP seat went to the SVP.
15009.m: From 1959 the magic formula shared the Federal Council seats among four parties.

15010.q: Which party got a seat in the Federal Council for the first time in 1943, with Ernst Nobs?
15010.e: Ernst Nobs was elected to the Federal Council on 15 December 1943 as the first Social Democrat.
15010.m: Ernst Nobs was the first SP Federal Councillor in 1943.

15011.q: What does concordance mean in Swiss politics?
a: As many major parties as possible take part in government.
The Federal Council is chosen by lot.
15011.e: Concordance is an unwritten principle: the big parties should all be represented together in the Federal Council.
15011.m: Concordance means that the big parties govern together.

15012.q: Who does the National Council represent first and foremost?
15012.e: The National Council is the chamber of the people. Its seats are shared out among the cantons according to population.
15012.m: The National Council represents the people.

15013.q: How are the 200 National Council seats shared out among the cantons?
a: Each canton gets the same number
According to the age of the canton
15013.e: Cantons with more people get more seats. But every canton is entitled to at least one seat.
15013.m: National Council seats depend on the population of the cantons.

15014.q: Which canton has the most seats in the National Council?
15014.e: Zurich is the canton with the largest population and had 36 seats in the 2023 elections.
15014.m: Zurich has the most members of the National Council.

15015.q: What is the minimum number of seats each canton has in the National Council?
15015.e: Even very small cantons such as Uri or Appenzell Innerrhoden have at least one seat in the National Council.
15015.m: Every canton has at least one seat in the National Council.

15016.q: How often is the National Council elected?
15016.e: The National Council is elected by the people every four years in October, most recently in October 2023.
15016.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

15017.q: Which voting system has been used to elect the National Council since 1919?
15017.e: Since 1919 the seats have been shared out in proportion to the parties’ votes. As a result the Free Democrats lost their absolute majority.
15017.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

15018.q: How many members does the National Council have today?
15018.e: The National Council has 200 members. Together with the 46 members of the Council of States, that makes 246 members of parliament.

15019.q: How many women were elected in 1971 as the first women members of the National Council?
15019.e: In the first elections with women’s suffrage in 1971, eleven women entered the National Council.
15019.m: In 1971 the first eleven women were elected to the National Council.

15020.q: What does each canton form in the National Council elections?
15020.e: In the National Council elections each canton is one constituency. The parties put up lists in each canton.
15020.m: Each canton is one constituency in National Council elections.

15021.q: How many times a year do the regular sessions of Parliament take place?
15021.e: Parliament meets four times a year for sessions of three weeks each: in spring, summer, autumn and winter.
15021.m: Parliament meets four times a year in sessions.

15022.q: What is another name for the National Council?
15022.e: Because it is much larger than the Council of States, with 200 members, the National Council is also called the Large Chamber.
15022.m: The National Council is also called the Large Chamber.

15023.q: Who does the Council of States represent?
15023.e: The Council of States is the chamber of the cantons. Each canton has almost the same weight, whatever its size.
15023.m: The Council of States represents the cantons.

15024.q: How many members of the Council of States does a canton like Zurich or Uri have?
15024.e: In the Council of States population does not count: big Zurich and little Uri each have two seats.
15024.m: Large and small cantons have the same number of seats in the Council of States.

15025.q: Which cantons have only one seat in the Council of States?
a: The former half-cantons such as Basel-Stadt
The border cantons such as Geneva
The mountain cantons such as the Grisons
The lake cantons such as Zug
15025.e: Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have one seat in the Council of States.
15025.m: The six former half-cantons each have one seat in the Council of States.

15026.q: What is the assembly called when the National Council and the Council of States meet together?
15026.e: Together, the members of the National Council and the Council of States form the United Federal Assembly. It elects the Federal Council, for example.
15026.m: The United Federal Assembly is made up of both chambers.

15027.q: How many members does the United Federal Assembly have?
15027.e: 200 members of the National Council and 46 of the Council of States add up to 246.
15027.m: The United Federal Assembly has 246 members.

15028.q: Who decides how the members of the Council of States are elected?
15028.e: The Federal Constitution leaves the voting procedure to the cantons. Today the people elect the members of the Council of States in all cantons.
15028.m: Each canton decides for itself how it elects its members of the Council of States.

15029.q: Who elects the members of the Council of States in the cantons today?
15029.e: In the past, the cantonal parliaments elected the members of the Council of States in some cantons. Today the people elect them everywhere.
15029.m: Members of the Council of States are elected by the people today.

15030.q: What rights does the Council of States have compared with the National Council?
15030.e: Both chambers have equal rights. A law is only passed if both the National Council and the Council of States agree.
15030.m: The National Council and the Council of States have equal rights.

15031.q: What happens to a new law if the National Council says yes but the Council of States says no?
a: It only applies in large cantons
15031.e: A law needs the approval of both councils. If they still cannot agree after several rounds of debate, the law has failed.
15031.m: A law needs a yes from both the National Council and the Council of States.

15032.q: In which year could women be elected to the Council of States for the first time?
15032.e: In 1971 women in Switzerland got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level. In the same year the first woman was elected to the Council of States.
15032.m: Since 1971 women can be elected to the Council of States.

15033.q: What is another name for the Council of States?
15033.e: With 46 members, the Council of States is much smaller than the National Council and is therefore called the Small Chamber.
15033.m: The Council of States is also called the Small Chamber.

15034.q: Within what time limit must the signatures for an optional referendum be collected?
15034.e: After a law is published, there are 100 days left for the referendum.

15035.q: What is the aim of a popular initiative?
a: To propose a change to the Federal Constitution
To stop a law passed by Parliament afterwards
15035.e: With a popular initiative, citizens can demand an addition to or change in the Federal Constitution. With a referendum, on the other hand, laws are stopped.
15035.m: With a popular initiative the people propose a change to the constitution.

15036.q: What is the “double majority” in votes on the constitution?
a: A majority of the people and a majority of the cantons
A majority in the National Council and in the Federal Council
Two votes on the same day
15036.e: A change to the constitution is only accepted if both the majority of voters (popular majority) and the majority of the cantons (cantonal majority) agree.
15036.m: Changes to the constitution need the popular majority and the cantonal majority.

15037.q: When must there always be a popular vote in Switzerland (mandatory referendum)?
a: For every change to the Federal Constitution
15037.e: Every change to the Federal Constitution must be put to the people and the cantons. That is why this referendum is called mandatory.
15037.m: Changes to the constitution always go to the people.

15038.q: How often do national votes usually take place in Switzerland?
15038.e: Each year the Confederation usually sets four voting Sundays. Several proposals can be voted on on one Sunday.
15038.m: National votes usually take place four times a year.

15040.q: When did Swiss men approve votes for women at federal level?
15040.e: On 7 February 1971 men approved votes for women with around 66 per cent voting yes. A first attempt had failed in 1959.
15040.m: Since 1971 women in Switzerland have been able to vote and be elected at federal level.

15041.q: Which canton had to be forced by the Federal Supreme Court in 1990 to give women the vote?
15041.e: The Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Innerrhoden still rejected votes for women in April 1990. In November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that this was against the constitution.
15041.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to give women the vote, in 1990.

15042.q: From what age can you vote and stand for election at federal level in Switzerland?
15042.e: Since 1991 the voting age at federal level has been 18; before that it was 20.
15042.m: At federal level you can vote from the age of 18.

15043.q: In which two cantons is there still a Landsgemeinde today?
15043.e: At the Landsgemeinde, voters gather in the open air and vote by raising their hands. Today this only happens in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
15043.m: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still hold a Landsgemeinde.

15044.q: What is heated in a steam engine to make steam?
15044.e: In the boiler, water is heated so much that it turns into steam. The steam pushes a piston back and forth. Thomas Newcomen built the first usable steam engine in 1712.
15044.m: In a steam engine, hot steam drives a piston.

15045.q: What were Newcomen’s first steam engines mainly used for?
15045.e: Water kept flooding into the coal mines. Newcomen’s engine pumped this water out so the miners could dig deeper.
15045.m: The first steam engines pumped water out of mines.

15046.q: Who improved the steam engine so that it needed much less coal?
15046.e: James Watt improved the steam engine and patented it in 1769. His engine used much less coal than Newcomen’s old one.
15046.m: James Watt made the steam engine more economical.

15047.q: Which important improvement did James Watt make to the steam engine?
15047.e: Watt let the steam cool in a separate container, the condenser. This kept the cylinder hot, and the engine wasted much less energy.
15047.m: Thanks to James Watt’s separate condenser, the steam engine saved a lot of coal.

15048.q: Which fuel was mainly burned in the steam engines of industrialisation?
15048.e: Under the boiler of a steam engine, hard coal usually burned. That is why coal regions like those in England or the Ruhr became centres of industry.
15048.m: Steam engines were mainly heated with coal.

15049.q: Which unit of power is named after James Watt?
15049.e: In honour of James Watt, the unit of power is called the “watt”. Today you can find it, for example, on every light bulb or hairdryer.
15049.m: The unit watt is named after the inventor James Watt.

15050.q: Which unit of power did James Watt introduce to compare his engines with working animals?
15050.e: Watt wanted to show how many horses his engine could replace. So he converted its power into horsepower (hp).
15050.m: Horsepower (hp) showed how many horses an engine could replace.

15051.q: Why was the steam engine so important for factories?
a: Factories no longer had to be by a river.
15051.e: Before, water wheels drove the machines, so factories were by rivers. With the steam engine, factories could be built anywhere, for example in towns.
15051.m: With the steam engine, factories were no longer tied to rivers.

15052.q: In which country did industrialisation begin in the second half of the 18th century?
15052.e: Great Britain had plenty of coal and iron, money from traders and many inventors. That is why the Industrial Revolution began there.

15053.q: What is the great change called in which machines increasingly replaced handwork?
15053.e: From about 1750, machines, factories and steam power greatly changed people’s work and lives. This change is called the Industrial Revolution.
15053.m: The Industrial Revolution changed work and life through machines.

15054.q: Which new means of transport was driven by a steam engine in the 19th century?
15054.e: A locomotive is a steam engine on wheels. It pulled railway carriages over long distances.
15054.m: The steam locomotive brought steam power onto the rails.

15055.q: What drove the first steamships forward?
15055.e: The steam engine turned large paddle wheels at the side or the back. In 1807 Robert Fulton made the steamship a success with the “Clermont”.
15055.m: Early steamships were driven by paddle wheels.

15056.q: Which spinning machine did James Hargreaves invent in 1764?
15056.e: With the spinning jenny one person could spin several threads at once. This made spinning much faster.
15056.m: The spinning jenny of 1764 spun several threads at once.

15057.q: In which branch of industry did the first factories of industrialisation appear?
15057.e: The first factories spun and wove cotton. Yarn and cloth could be made much faster with machines than by hand.
15057.m: The first factories made yarn and cloth.

15058.q: What changed when power looms came in?
a: Cloth could be woven much faster.
Cloth was only made of paper.
15058.e: Power looms were driven by machines. So much more cloth was made in a short time than by hand, and many hand weavers lost their work.
15058.m: Power looms made weaving much faster.

15059.q: What does “division of labour” mean in a factory?
a: Each worker does only one particular step of the work.
Each worker makes a whole product alone.
The workers share their wages equally.
The workers take turns working at home.
15059.e: In the factory, production was split into many small steps. Each worker repeated the same task over and over, which made production faster.
15059.m: With division of labour, each person does only one small step.

15060.q: What is the way of working before factories called, in which families spun and wove at home for a merchant?
15060.e: Many families, including in the Zurich Oberland, spun and wove in their own living rooms. A merchant brought the raw material and collected the finished goods.
15060.m: Before factories, many families worked at home.

15061.q: What were the workers in England called who destroyed machines around 1811 and 1812 because they feared for their jobs?
15061.e: The machine breakers, also called Luddites in England, smashed weaving machines. They feared that the machines would take away their work and wages.
15061.m: Machine breakers destroyed machines because they feared for their jobs.

15062.q: How long did factory workers often work each day at the beginning of industrialisation?
15062.e: At first there were hardly any laws to protect workers. Working days of 12 to 16 hours, Saturdays included, were normal.
15062.m: In the past factory workers often worked 12 to 16 hours a day.

15063.q: What is the growth of towns called, as many people moved from the countryside to the factory towns?
15063.e: Factories needed many workers, so people moved from the countryside to the towns. The towns grew very quickly, often with cramped and dirty housing areas.
15063.m: Industrialisation made the towns grow strongly.

15064.q: Who introduced the assembly line in car production in 1913?
15064.e: From 1913 Henry Ford had his Model T built on an assembly line. This made cars much faster and cheaper to produce.
15064.m: Henry Ford introduced the assembly line in car production in 1913.

15065.q: Which English city became the centre of the textile industry because of its many cotton mills?
15065.e: In the 19th century Manchester had countless cotton mills. The city became the symbol of industrialisation.
15065.m: Manchester was the centre of the English cotton industry.

15066.q: What did a set of factory rules regulate in the 19th century?
a: The workers’ hours, duties and punishments
The prices of goods in shops
The election of the factory owner
15066.e: The factory rules contained strict rules, for example about when you had to turn up. Anyone who came late or chatted often had money taken off their wages.
15066.m: The factory rules set strict rules for the workers.

15067.q: Why were many early spinning mills by rivers?
a: The yarn had to float in the river.
15067.e: The first large spinning machines were driven by water power. That is why spinning mills were built by rivers, in Switzerland too, for example in the Zurich Oberland.
15067.m: Early spinning mills used water power.

15068.q: In which country did the first public railway with steam locomotives run in 1825?
15068.e: The Stockton and Darlington Railway in England opened in 1825. It mainly carried coal from the mines to the ports.
15068.m: The first public steam railway ran in England in 1825.

15069.q: Roughly what was the top speed of the famous locomotive “Rocket” of 1829?
15069.e: Robert Stephenson’s “Rocket” reached almost 50 kilometres per hour. At that time that was faster than any horse-drawn coach.
15069.m: The “Rocket” was faster than any coach.

15070.q: What was new when the railway from Liverpool to Manchester opened in 1830?
a: It was meant for passengers and ran to a timetable.
15070.e: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. It carried passengers and goods to a fixed timetable and became a model for many railways.
15070.m: The Liverpool to Manchester railway became a model in 1830.

15071.q: Which engineer is known as the “Father of Railways” and built locomotives with his son Robert?
15071.e: George Stephenson built locomotives and railway lines in England. Together with his son Robert he strongly shaped early railway building.
15071.m: George Stephenson is known as the “Father of Railways”.

15072.q: What is the distance between the two rails of a track called?
15072.e: The gauge is the distance between the rails. The most common gauge in the world is standard gauge at 1,435 millimetres, which is also used by SBB, the Swiss Federal Railways.
15072.m: The distance between the rails is called the gauge.

15073.q: Which country did the locomotive “Adler” of the first German railway in 1835 come from?
15073.e: England was far ahead in building railways. So a locomotive from England was bought for the first German railway from Nuremberg to Fürth.
15073.m: The first locomotives in Germany came from England.

15074.q: How did the railway change trade in the 19th century?
a: Goods could be transported faster and more cheaply.
Goods could only be carried by horses.
Goods became much dearer and slower.
15074.e: By rail, coal, grain and factory goods could be moved quickly in large amounts. This lowered prices and helped industry.
15074.m: The railway made transporting goods faster and cheaper.

15075.q: What was the name of the first railway line that lay entirely on Swiss soil?
15075.e: The Swiss Northern Railway linked Zurich with Baden. People call it the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” (Spanish Roll Railway), after a pastry from Baden.
15075.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn was the first railway entirely on Swiss soil.

15076.q: In which year did the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden open?
15076.e: The line was officially opened on 7 August 1847. It was about 23 kilometres long.
15076.m: From 1847 the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn ran from Zurich to Baden.

15077.q: Which railway line already reached Swiss soil in 1844?
a: The railway from Strasbourg to Basel
The railway from Milan to Lugano
The railway from Geneva to Lausanne
The railway from Vienna to St Gallen
15077.e: In 1844 the Alsace railway linked Strasbourg with Basel. It was the first railway to reach Swiss territory, but lay mostly in France.
15077.m: As early as 1844 a railway ran from Strasbourg to Basel.

15078.q: Where does the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden get its name from?
15078.e: The “Spanische Brötli” (Spanish rolls) were a fine pastry from Baden. Thanks to the railway they arrived in Zurich still fresh for breakfast.
15078.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn is named after a pastry from Baden.

15079.q: In which year were the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) founded?
15079.e: Before, Swiss railways belonged to private companies. The SBB were created in 1902, when the Confederation took over the large private railways.

15080.q: Which important source of energy did Swiss factories use, because Switzerland has hardly any coal?
15080.e: Switzerland has hardly any coal of its own, but many rivers and streams. That is why many spinning mills stood by rivers and used water wheels and turbines.
15080.m: Swiss factories mainly used water power.

15081.q: Which industry was the most important in Switzerland at the beginning of industrialisation?
15081.e: Spinning mills, weaving mills and embroidery works employed a great many people in Switzerland. Centres included Zurich, the Zurich Oberland, Glarus and eastern Switzerland.
15081.m: In Switzerland industrialisation began with the textile industry.

15082.q: What did Swiss engineering works such as Escher Wyss or Sulzer make in the 19th century?
15082.e: Many engineering works started as spinning mills and first built their own textile machines. Later they made turbines, steam engines and steamships.
15082.m: In Switzerland spinning mills grew into engineering works.

15083.q: What happened in 1832 in the Uster fire in the Zurich Oberland?
a: Home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill.
Lightning destroyed the church in Uster.
The town of Uster burned down in a war.
A steam locomotive exploded in the station.
15083.e: On 22 November 1832 home workers set fire to the Corrodi & Pfister spinning and weaving mill in Oberuster. They feared that the weaving machines would take away their work.
15083.m: In the Uster fire of 1832, home weavers destroyed a factory out of fear for their jobs.

15084.q: Which Zurich politician and businessman founded railways and a major bank and supported ETH?
15084.e: Alfred Escher was one of the most powerful men in Switzerland in the 19th century. He worked for railways, a big bank and the Gotthard Railway.
15084.m: Alfred Escher was an important pioneer of modern Switzerland.

15085.q: In which year did the Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich begin teaching?
15085.e: ETH began in 1855 as the “Polytechnikum”. It trained engineers, whom Switzerland urgently needed for railways and factories.

15086.q: Which industry is the Jura Arc in Switzerland especially known for?
15086.e: In the Jura, for example in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle or Biel, many watch factories were set up. Swiss watches were sold all over the world.
15086.m: The Jura Arc is a centre of the Swiss watch industry.

15087.q: In which Swiss city did a large chemical industry grow up in the 19th century, starting with dyes?
15087.e: In Basel, companies first made dyes for the textile industry. This later developed into the large pharmaceutical industry.
15087.m: Basel became the centre of Swiss chemistry.

15088.q: Which product was eastern Switzerland around St Gallen world-famous for in the 19th century?
15088.e: St Gallen embroidery was exported to many countries. For a time embroidery was one of Switzerland’s most important exports.
15088.m: St Gallen was world-famous for its embroidery.

15089.q: Which bank did Alfred Escher found in 1856 to finance railway building?
15089.e: Building railways was expensive and needed a lot of money. So in 1856 Alfred Escher founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, which later became Credit Suisse.
15089.m: Alfred Escher founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt in 1856.

15090.q: What did the first mechanical spinning mills in Switzerland make?
15090.e: In spinning mills, machines twisted cotton into yarn. One of the first successful ones was the Hard spinning mill near Winterthur around 1802.
15090.m: Spinning mills used machines to make yarn from cotton.

15091.q: Why did many people emigrate from Switzerland to America in the 19th century?
a: Because of poverty and lack of work
Because of a war in Switzerland
Because there was no work in America
15091.e: Many home workers lost their income because of the machines, and there were bad harvests. So many looked for a better life overseas.
15091.m: Poverty drove many Swiss to emigrate in the 19th century.

15092.q: In which year did the Gotthard Railway open in full?
15092.e: On 1 June 1882 the whole Gotthard Railway went into service. It linked German-speaking Switzerland directly with Ticino and Italy.

15093.q: Roughly how long is the old Gotthard railway tunnel from Göschenen to Airolo?
15093.e: The summit tunnel is about 15 kilometres long. When it opened, it was the longest railway tunnel in the world.
15093.m: The old Gotthard tunnel is about 15 kilometres long.

15094.q: When did the tunnel builders from the north and south meet in the breakthrough of the Gotthard tunnel?
15094.e: After more than seven years of work, the two tunnels met inside the mountain on 29 February 1880. They were only very slightly out of line.
15094.m: The breakthrough in the Gotthard tunnel happened in 1880.

15095.q: Which builder from Geneva led the building of the Gotthard tunnel but did not live to see the breakthrough?
15095.e: Louis Favre died of heart failure in the tunnel on 19 July 1879. He did not live to see the breakthrough half a year later.
15095.m: Louis Favre built the Gotthard tunnel and died in 1879 before the breakthrough.

15096.q: Which country did most of the workers building the Gotthard tunnel come from?
15096.e: Most of the miners came from poor areas in Piedmont and Lombardy. They worked in very hard and dangerous conditions.
15096.m: The Gotthard tunnel was built mainly by Italian workers.

15097.q: Roughly how many workers died building the Gotthard tunnel?
15097.e: During the building work 199 workers died, many from wagons, falling rocks or explosives. Many more died later of illness and injuries.
15097.m: About 200 workers died building the Gotthard tunnel.

15098.q: What happened during the strike of the tunnel workers in Göschenen in 1875?
a: Armed men fired into the crowd and four workers died.
The workers immediately got double pay.
Building the tunnel was stopped for ever.
The workers took over running the building work.
15098.e: On 27 July 1875 the workers went on strike for more pay and better conditions. A police unit from Altdorf fired into the crowd, and four Italian workers died.
15098.m: During the strike in Göschenen in 1875 four workers were shot dead.

15099.q: What is the village of Wassen on the Gotthard Railway known for?
a: From the train you see its church three times from different heights.
It has the highest railway station in Europe.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel starts there.
The first locomotive was built there.
15099.e: Near Wassen the railway climbs the slope with loops and spiral tunnels. The church on a rocky ledge can be seen from all three levels of the line.
15099.m: At Wassen you see the church three times thanks to spiral tunnels.

15100.q: Why was the Gotthard Railway switched to electric power?
a: Coal was scarce in the First World War.
15100.e: Switzerland had to buy coal from abroad, and during the war it was scarce and expensive. Electricity from water power, on the other hand, was available in the country itself.
15100.m: The Gotthard Railway runs on electricity from water power.

15101.q: How long is the Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016?
15101.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long and opened on 1 June 2016. It is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
15101.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long.

15102.q: Which neighbouring countries helped to pay for building the Gotthard Railway?
15102.e: The Gotthard Railway was also important for trade between north and south. That is why Italy and Germany shared the costs.
15102.m: Italy and Germany helped pay for the Gotthard Railway.

15103.q: What was Alfred Escher’s role in the Gotthard Railway?
a: He was president of the Gotthard Railway Company.
He dug the tunnel as a miner.
15103.e: Alfred Escher campaigned hard for the Gotthard line and led the Gotthard Railway Company. Because of a financial crisis he resigned in 1879.
15103.m: Alfred Escher led the Gotthard Railway Company.

15104.q: When did work start on the Gotthard railway tunnel?
15104.e: In autumn 1872 work began at both tunnel entrances, in Göschenen and Airolo. After about seven and a half years the two sides broke through.
15104.m: Work on the Gotthard Tunnel began in 1872.

15105.q: In which workplaces did children especially often have to work during industrialisation?
15105.e: In textile factories children tied broken threads back together. In mines they crawled through narrow tunnels because they were small.
15105.m: Children often worked in spinning mills and mines.

15106.q: Why did factory owners like to employ children?
a: Children were paid much lower wages.
15106.e: Children earned only a fraction of an adult’s wage. Even so, many poor families needed their earnings to survive.
15106.m: Child labour was cheap for factory owners.

15107.q: Why were children particularly suited to certain jobs in mines?
a: They were small and could fit through narrow tunnels.
They could see better in the dark.
They did not need air to breathe.
15107.e: Many passages in the coal mines were very low. Small children pulled carts there or opened ventilation doors, often for hours in the dark.
15107.m: Small children often had to work in narrow mine tunnels.

15108.q: Which country was the first to appoint state factory inspectors to protect children, with a Factory Act in 1833?
15108.e: The British Factory Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from working in textile factories and limited the working hours of older ones. For the first time, paid inspectors checked that the rules were followed.
15108.m: Great Britain appointed factory inspectors to protect children in 1833.

15109.q: From what age were children allowed to work in factories in Switzerland under the Factory Act of 1877?
15109.e: The federal Factory Act banned factory work for children under 14. This gave them more time for school.
15109.m: From 1877, children under 14 were not allowed to work in Swiss factories.

15110.q: What was the longest a working day in a factory could last under the Swiss Factory Act of 1877?
15110.e: The Factory Act introduced the 11-hour day. There were also rules against night and Sunday work.
15110.m: The Factory Act of 1877 limited the working day to 11 hours.

15111.q: How was the federal Factory Act of 1877 introduced?
a: The people narrowly approved it in a vote.
A king ordered it without a vote.
The factory owners wrote it on their own.
15111.e: On 21 October 1877 Swiss men voted on the law. It was passed with only 51.5 per cent voting yes.
15111.m: The people narrowly approved the Factory Act in 1877.

15112.q: Under the Swiss Factory Act of 1877, who checked that the rules were being followed?
15112.e: The law created a federal factory inspectorate. The inspectors visited factories and checked things like working hours.
15112.m: Factory inspectors made sure the Factory Act was followed.

15113.q: Which canton issued one of the first Swiss regulations against child labour in spinning mills in 1815?
15113.e: The Zurich regulation of 1815 banned children under 9 from factory work and also from night work. However, these rules could hardly be enforced.
15113.m: Zurich issued a regulation against child labour as early as 1815.

15114.q: What problem was often caused by child labour in factories?
a: The children could not go to school regularly.
The children had to do military service.
The children were not allowed to live with their parents.
The children had to pay taxes.
15114.e: Anyone standing in a factory for long hours could not go to school. In Prussia too, the breach of compulsory schooling was a main reason for the first protective laws.
15114.m: Child labour often stopped children from going to school.

15115.q: Which Swiss canton introduced the 12-hour day for adult factory workers too, with a Factory Act in 1864?
15115.e: In the textile canton of Glarus, the Landsgemeinde (open-air assembly) passed a Factory Act in 1864 against the government’s wishes, with a 12-hour day and a ban on night work. It is seen as a milestone in protecting workers, and the later federal Factory Act was based on the Glarus rules.
15115.m: Glarus introduced the 12-hour factory day by Landsgemeinde vote in 1864.

15116.q: Who were the “Verdingkinder” (contract children) in Switzerland?
a: Children who had to work for other families
Children who served in the army
15116.e: Poor or orphaned children were often sent to farming families, where they had to work hard. Many of them suffered great injustice, which Switzerland is now coming to terms with.
15116.m: Verdingkinder had to work for other families.

15117.q: With which sentence does “The Communist Manifesto” end?
15117.e: This call was meant to bring workers of all countries together. The sentence became a well-known slogan of the labour movement.
15117.m: The Communist Manifesto ends with “Workers of the world, unite!”

a: a group of employees working together for better working conditions
15118.e: In a trade union, workers join forces. Together they can fight more effectively for higher wages and shorter working hours.
15118.m: Trade unions stand up together for employees’ rights.

a: The factory is sold to a new owner.
15119.e: In a strike, many people stop working at the same time. In this way they put pressure on employers to meet their demands.
15119.m: In a strike, workers stop working together.

15120.q: In the 19th century, what was the name for workers’ many problems, such as poverty, illness and poor housing?
15120.e: With industrialisation, many working families lived in great hardship. How to solve this hardship was called the social question.
15120.m: The hardship of workers was called the social question.

15122.q: When it was founded in 1888, whose situation did the Social Democratic Party (SP) mainly want to improve?
15122.e: The SP was founded in 1888. It wanted to improve the situation of working people by democratic means, for example with shorter working hours and better wages.
15122.m: From the start, the SP stood up for workers.

15123.q: When did the general strike take place in Switzerland?
15123.e: From 12 to 14 November 1918, around 250,000 workers went on strike. It was the biggest strike in Swiss history.
15123.m: The general strike took place in November 1918.

15124.q: Who led the 1918 general strike as president of the Olten Action Committee?
15124.e: Robert Grimm was president of the Olten Action Committee. Because of the call to strike, he was sentenced to six months in prison in 1919.
15124.m: Robert Grimm led the general strike of 1918.

15125.q: Which demand of the 1918 general strike was put into practice in industry as early as 1919 and 1920?
15125.e: The 48-hour week was introduced in industry in 1919 and 1920. Women’s right to vote at federal level, on the other hand, only came in 1971.
15125.m: The 48-hour week was introduced soon after the general strike.

15126.q: Which social insurance, demanded during the 1918 general strike, only came into force in 1948?
15126.e: Old-age and survivors’ insurance (AHV) was one of the demands of the general strike. In the end it only came into force in 1948.
15126.m: The AHV was demanded in 1918 and introduced in 1948.

15127.q: What did the Federal Council use against the general strike in 1918?
15127.e: The Federal Council called up soldiers and gave the strikers an ultimatum. After three days the strike leaders called off the general strike. In Grenchen, three young workers were shot dead.
15127.m: The Federal Council ended the 1918 general strike with the army.

15128.q: Which day is known around the world as the labour movement’s “Labour Day”?
15128.e: On 1 May, trade unions in many countries demonstrate for employees’ rights. In some Swiss cantons it is a public holiday.

15129.q: What term did Marx and Engels use for the working class, which owns nothing but its ability to work?
15129.e: Proletarians do not own factories or machines. They live by selling their labour for wages.
15129.m: The proletariat is the working class that owns no property.

15130.q: Which Italian built the first usable battery, the voltaic pile, around 1800?
15130.e: Alessandro Volta presented his pile to the Royal Society in London in 1800. For the first time it produced a steady electric current.
15130.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

15131.q: Which unit of electrical voltage is named after Alessandro Volta?
15131.e: Voltage is measured in volts, in honour of Alessandro Volta. A plug socket in Switzerland, for example, has 230 volts.

15132.q: Which English scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
15132.e: In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that a moving magnet in a coil of wire produces electricity. Generators in power stations work on this principle.
15132.m: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831.

15133.q: What does a dynamo, like the one Werner von Siemens improved in 1866, produce?
15133.e: A dynamo turns movement into electricity. Werner von Siemens made it so powerful that electricity could be produced cheaply and in large amounts.
15133.m: A dynamo makes electricity from movement.

15134.q: Which American inventor received a patent for his light bulb in 1880 and had it mass-produced?
15134.e: Thomas Edison applied for a patent for his light bulb in 1879 and received it in 1880. He was not the only inventor, but he made the bulb practical and cheap.
15134.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb fit for everyday use.

15135.q: Which material did Edison soon use for especially long-lasting filaments?
15135.e: In his first successful experiment in 1879, Edison used a carbon filament. Later he used carbonised bamboo fibres from Japan, which lasted over 1,000 hours.
15135.m: Edison used carbonised bamboo for his filaments.

15136.q: Where did the first electric light in Switzerland shine in 1879?
a: in a hotel in St Moritz
in the Federal Palace in Bern
15136.e: On 18 July 1879 the hotelier Johannes Badrutt had electric arc lamps lit in the dining room of his Kulm Hotel in St Moritz. The electricity came from a small power plant of his own.
15136.m: Switzerland’s first electric light shone in St Moritz in 1879.

15137.q: From which energy source has Switzerland got most of its electricity for over a hundred years?
15137.e: Switzerland has many rivers and reservoirs in the Alps. That is why it built lots of hydroelectric power stations early on.
15137.m: Switzerland gets most of its electricity from hydropower.

15138.q: Why was hydropower in Switzerland also called “white coal”?
a: It replaced the coal the country lacked as a source of energy.
The water was pressed into white stones.
White coal was found in the Alps.
Coal was painted white before burning.
15138.e: Other countries had lots of coal for their industry, but Switzerland had hardly any. Water from the snow-covered mountains therefore became its most important source of energy.

15139.q: What advantage did the electric motor have over the steam engine in factories?
a: Each machine could have its own small drive.
It needed no energy at all.
It was much louder and more dangerous.
15139.e: A steam engine drove many machines at once through long belts. Electric motors were small and could drive each machine separately.
15139.m: Electric motors made powering factories simpler and more flexible.

15140.q: Which material became standard for light bulb filaments around 1910?
15140.e: Tungsten only melts at very high temperatures. That is why a tungsten filament lasts a long time and shines brightly.
15140.m: Filaments are usually made of tungsten.

15141.q: Was Thomas Edison the only inventor of the light bulb?
a: No, others such as Joseph Swan built light bulbs too.
Yes, nobody else was working on it.
No, the Romans already had light bulbs.
Yes, the idea was protected by law.
15141.e: The Englishman Joseph Swan showed a light bulb as early as February 1879. But Edison made it especially well known and cheap. In 1883 their companies merged.
15141.m: The light bulb had several inventors.

15142.q: How did electric light change life in towns and cities?
a: Streets and factories could be brightly lit at night too.
People had to go to bed earlier.
Candles suddenly became much more expensive.
Towns became completely dark at night.
15142.e: Electric lamps lit up the night without an open flame. Factories could work at night and streets became safer.
15142.m: Electric light made towns and factories bright at night too.

17022.e: Asia is the biggest continent. It has the most area.
17022.m: Asia is the biggest continent on Earth.

17023.e: Australia is the smallest continent. Most of it belongs to the country of Australia.

17024.e: A continent is a very large landmass. There are often many countries on it.
17024.m: A continent is a huge piece of land.

17025.e: The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean. Its name means “peaceful ocean”.
17025.m: The Pacific is the biggest ocean on Earth.

17026.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and America?
17026.e: The Atlantic separates Europe and Africa from America. Ships need many days to cross it.
17026.m: The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.

17027.q: What does the water in the ocean taste like?
17027.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. That is why you cannot drink it.
17027.m: The water in the ocean is salty.

17028.q: What colour are oceans usually on maps?
17028.e: On maps and globes, water is almost always drawn in blue. That way you recognise it at once.
17028.m: Oceans are usually blue on maps.

17029.q: Which country is the biggest in the world?
17029.e: Russia has the largest area of all countries. It lies in Europe and in Asia.
17029.m: Russia is the biggest country in the world by area.

17030.q: Which country is the smallest in the world?
17030.e: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre. The Pope lives there.
17030.m: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

17031.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is very small and lies to the east?
17031.e: Liechtenstein lies between Switzerland and Austria. It is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
17031.m: Liechtenstein is a small neighbouring country of Switzerland.

17032.q: What does the Swiss flag look like?
17032.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is square.
17032.m: The Swiss flag has a white cross on a red background.

17033.q: Which country has a white flag with a red circle?
17033.e: The red circle on the Japanese flag stands for the sun. Japan is also called the “Land of the Rising Sun”.
17033.m: The flag of Japan shows a red circle on white.

17034.q: How many stars does the flag of the USA have?
17034.e: Each of the 50 stars stands for one state of the USA. The 13 stripes are a reminder of the first colonies.
17034.m: The flag of the USA has 50 stars.

17035.q: In which city is the seat of the Swiss government?
17035.e: The Federal Council and Parliament work in Bern. Bern is called the federal city.

17036.q: What is the capital of Austria?
17036.e: Vienna is the capital and the largest city of Austria. The famous Schönbrunn Palace is there.
17036.m: Vienna is the capital of Austria.

17037.q: What is the capital of Spain?
17037.e: Madrid lies roughly in the middle of Spain. It is the largest city in the country.
17037.m: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

17038.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17038.e: Tokyo is the capital of Japan. A great many people live in the Tokyo region.
17038.m: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

17039.q: What money do people pay with in Switzerland?
17039.e: In Switzerland people pay with francs and centimes (Rappen). One franc has 100 Rappen.
17039.m: In Switzerland you pay with francs.

17040.q: What is the capital of Germany?
17040.e: Berlin is the capital and the largest city of Germany. The Brandenburg Gate is there.
17040.m: Berlin is the capital of Germany.

17041.q: What is the highest mountain in Germany called?
17041.e: The Zugspitze is about 2960 metres high. It lies on the border with Austria.
17041.m: The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.

17042.q: In which direction is Germany from Switzerland?
17042.e: Germany lies north of Switzerland. Basel and Schaffhausen are close to the border.
17042.m: Germany lies to the north of Switzerland.

17043.q: How many federal states does Germany have?
17043.e: Germany is divided into 16 federal states, for example Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

17044.q: In which city is the Eiffel Tower?
17044.e: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris. It is made of iron and is about 330 metres high.
17044.m: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris.

17045.q: What colours is the flag of France?
17045.e: The French flag has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red.
17045.m: The flag of France is blue, white and red.

17046.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the west of Switzerland?
17046.e: France lies to the west of Switzerland. The city of Geneva is right on the border with France.
17046.m: France lies to the west of Switzerland.

17047.q: What does Italy look like on the map?
17047.e: Italy is long and narrow and looks like a boot. The toe points into the Mediterranean.
17047.m: On the map, Italy looks like a boot.

17048.q: What is the capital of Italy?
17048.e: Rome is the capital of Italy. The Colosseum is there.
17048.m: Rome is the capital of Italy.

17049.q: Which dish originally comes from Italy?
17049.e: Pizza as we know it comes from Naples in Italy.

17050.q: In which Italian city do people travel by boat instead of by car?
17050.e: Venice is built on lots of small islands. Instead of roads there are canals and narrow lanes, and people travel by boat and gondola.
17050.m: In Venice people travel by boat on canals.

17051.q: Which sea lies to the south of Europe?
17051.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe and Africa. Many people go on beach holidays there.
17051.m: The Mediterranean lies to the south of Europe.

17052.q: Which mountain range forms a border between Europe and Asia?
17052.e: The Urals are a long mountain range in Russia. They are seen as the border between Europe and Asia.
17052.m: The Urals separate Europe and Asia.

17053.q: What is the money that people pay with in many countries of Europe called?
17053.e: Many countries in Europe share the euro as their money. Switzerland is not one of them.
17053.m: In many countries of Europe people pay with euros.

17054.q: What is the highest mountain in Africa called?
17054.e: Kilimanjaro is in Tanzania and is almost 5900 metres high. There is snow at the top, even though it is hot at the bottom.
17054.m: Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.

17055.q: In which African country are the famous pyramids of Giza?
17055.e: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt. They were built more than 4000 years ago.
17055.m: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt.

17056.q: Which big river flows through Egypt?
17056.e: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world. It flows through Egypt into the Mediterranean.

17057.q: Which animal lives in the wild in Africa?
17057.e: Giraffes live in the African savannah. With their long necks they eat leaves from tall trees.
17057.m: Giraffes live in the wild in Africa.

17058.q: In which country is the Great Wall?
17058.e: The Great Wall of China is a very long structure in China. It was built for protection against enemies.
17058.m: The Great Wall is in China.

17059.q: In which country do giant pandas live in the wild?
17059.e: Giant pandas live in mountain forests in China. They mainly eat bamboo.
17059.m: Giant pandas live in the wild in China.

17060.q: Which country has had the most inhabitants in the world since 2023?
17060.e: Since 2023, more people have lived in India than in any other country. There are over 1.4 billion (as of 2025).
17060.m: India has had the most inhabitants since 2023.

17061.q: On which continent do the most people live?
17061.e: More than half of all people live in Asia. Some very populous countries are there.

17062.q: Which two parts make up America?
17062.e: America is made up of North America and South America. Central America lies in between.
17062.m: America is made up of North America and South America.

17063.q: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
17063.e: The Statue of Liberty stands on a small island near New York. France gave it to the USA as a gift.
17063.m: The Statue of Liberty is in New York.

17064.q: Which is the biggest country in South America?
17064.e: Brazil is the biggest country in South America. People there speak Portuguese.
17064.m: Brazil is the biggest country in South America.

17065.q: Who came to America by ship in 1492?
17065.e: Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492. He reached islands off America.

17066.q: Which animal carries its baby in a pouch and lives in Australia?
17066.e: The kangaroo is a marsupial. The baby grows up in its mother's pouch.
17066.m: The kangaroo lives in Australia and has a pouch.

17067.q: Which animal sleeps a lot and eats eucalyptus leaves?
17067.e: The koala lives in Australia in eucalyptus trees. It sleeps almost all day.

17068.q: What is the capital of Australia?
17068.e: Many people think of Sydney, but the capital is Canberra. Sydney is the biggest city.
17068.m: Canberra is the capital of Australia.

17069.q: What is the famous red rock in Australia called?
17069.e: Uluru is a huge red rock in the middle of Australia. It is sacred to the Aboriginal people.
17069.m: Uluru is a big red rock in Australia.

17070.q: What is Antarctica almost completely covered with?
17070.e: Antarctica is almost completely covered by a thick layer of ice. In many places the ice is kilometres thick.
17070.m: Antarctica is covered with thick ice.

17071.e: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim well. Many species live in the south, for example in Antarctica.

17072.q: Who lives in Antarctica for a while?
17072.e: There are no towns in Antarctica. Researchers live there in stations and study the ice and weather.
17072.m: Researchers live in stations in Antarctica.

17073.q: What is the weather usually like in Antarctica?
17073.e: Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth. Temperatures below minus 80 degrees have been measured there.
17073.m: It is very cold in Antarctica.

17074.q: What is the highest mountain in the world called?
17074.e: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas. It is about 8849 metres high.
17074.m: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

17075.q: Which pointed mountain stands near Zermatt?
17075.e: The Matterhorn is in Valais near Zermatt. Its pyramid shape is known all over the world.

17076.q: What do you call the highest point of a mountain?
17076.e: The summit is the very top of a mountain. There is often a summit cross there.
17076.m: The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.

17077.q: What do you call the place where a river begins?
17077.e: At the source, the water often comes out of the ground. From there it flows on as a stream.
17077.m: A river begins at its source.

17078.e: The Rhine flows through Basel and then on into Germany. Basel has a Rhine port.

17079.q: Which sea does the Rhone flow into?
17079.e: The Rhone begins at the Rhone Glacier in Valais. It flows through France into the Mediterranean.
17079.m: The Rhone flows into the Mediterranean.

17080.q: Which river flows through the city of Bern?
17080.e: In Bern the Aare makes a big loop around the old town. In summer lots of people swim in it.

17081.q: Which lake is the largest in Switzerland?
17081.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland. Part of it belongs to France.
17081.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.

17082.q: Which lake do Switzerland, Germany and Austria all border?
17082.e: Lake Constance lies between three countries. Towns such as Konstanz and Bregenz are on its shores.

17083.q: Which lake is the city of Lucerne on?
17083.e: Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne. Many boats sail across the lake from there.

17084.q: What kind of water do most lakes have?
17084.e: Most lakes are filled with fresh water. There is hardly any salt in it.

17085.q: Does Switzerland have a coastline on the sea?
17085.e: Switzerland is a landlocked country. That means it has no access to the sea.
17085.m: Switzerland is not by the sea.

17086.q: In which sea can you float on top almost without swimming?
17086.e: The Dead Sea is extremely salty. All that salt holds your body up, so you float on top.
17086.m: In the Dead Sea you float on top because of the salt.

17087.q: What is it called when the sea goes back from the beach?
17087.e: At low tide the water level drops and the beach gets wider. At high tide the water rises again.
17087.m: At low tide the sea goes back.

a: Land surrounded by water on all sides
17088.e: An island is a piece of land completely surrounded by water. You can often only reach it by ship or plane.
17088.m: An island is surrounded by water on all sides.

17089.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
17089.e: Greenland is the largest island in the world. Most of it is covered with ice.
17089.m: Greenland is the largest island in the world.

17090.q: Which large island lies off the east coast of Africa?
17090.e: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean off Africa. Lemurs live there.
17090.m: Madagascar lies off the coast of Africa.

17091.e: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and belongs to Italy. The volcano Etna is there.
17091.m: Sicily is an island of Italy.

17092.q: Which animal often carries loads in the desert?
17092.e: Camels can go a long time without water. That is why they are good pack animals in the desert.
17092.m: The camel is a pack animal in the desert.

17093.q: What do you call a place with water and palm trees in the desert?
17093.e: In an oasis there is water from the ground. That is why plants such as date palms grow there.
17093.m: An oasis is a place with water in the desert.

17094.q: What is there very little of in a desert?
17094.e: It hardly ever rains in the desert. That is why only a few plants grow there.
17094.m: It rains very little in the desert.

17095.q: What is the largest rainforest in the world called?
17095.e: The Amazon rainforest is in South America. It is the largest rainforest on Earth.
17095.m: The Amazon rainforest is the largest rainforest.

17096.q: What is the weather like in the tropical rainforest?
17096.e: It is warm all year in the tropical rainforest. It rains almost every day.
17096.m: The tropical rainforest is warm and wet.

17097.q: Which animal lives in the rainforest?
17097.e: Very many kinds of animals live in the rainforest. Colourful parrots live high up in the trees.

17098.e: People cut down trees for wood, fields and pastures. So a lot of rainforest disappears every year.
17098.m: Rainforests are getting smaller because trees are cut down.

17099.q: Which large predator lives near the North Pole?
17099.e: Polar bears live in the Arctic around the North Pole. They mainly hunt seals.
17099.m: Polar bears live in the Arctic.

17100.q: What do you stand on at the North Pole?
17100.e: There is no land at the North Pole. A layer of ice floats on the sea there.
17100.m: At the North Pole you stand on ice over the sea.

17101.q: Which way does the needle of a compass point?
17101.e: The compass needle is magnetic and points north. That is how you find your way.

17102.q: On which continent is the South Pole?
17102.e: The South Pole lies in the middle of the continent of Antarctica. There are no towns and no trees there.
17102.m: The South Pole is in Antarctica.

17103.q: Who was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911?
17103.e: The Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole with dog sleds in December 1911. The Briton Robert Scott got there about a month later.
17103.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911.

17104.q: Roughly how long does it stay dark at the South Pole in winter?
17104.e: At the South Pole the sun does not rise for about half a year in winter. In summer, on the other hand, it shines non-stop for about half a year.
17104.m: At the South Pole the winter night lasts about half a year.

17105.e: A globe shows the Earth as a small ball. That way you can see countries and seas in their correct positions.
17105.m: A globe is a model of the Earth.

17106.e: The Earth is round like a ball. That is why a globe is also shaped like a sphere.
17106.m: A globe is shaped like a sphere.

17107.q: What is the line that runs around the middle of the globe called?
17107.e: The equator divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half. In lowlands near the equator it is warm all year.
17107.m: The equator runs around the middle of the Earth.

17108.q: What does a world map show?
17108.e: A world map shows all the continents and seas on a flat sheet.
17108.m: A world map shows the whole Earth on a flat sheet.

17109.q: What do you call a book with lots of maps?
17109.e: In an atlas you find maps of countries, continents and the whole world.
17109.m: A book with lots of maps is called an atlas.

17110.q: Which compass direction is at the top of most maps?
17110.e: On most maps north is at the top and south at the bottom. East is on the right, west on the left.
17110.m: On most maps north is at the top.

17111.q: Which country lies entirely in Europe and is the largest by area?
17111.e: Ukraine is about 600,000 km² in size. Russia is bigger, but most of it lies in Asia.
17111.m: Ukraine is the largest country that lies entirely in Europe.

17112.q: Which of these countries does not border Switzerland?
17112.e: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. Belgium lies further to the north-west.

17113.q: Which country in the European Union has the most inhabitants?
17113.e: Germany has over 80 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That makes it the most populous country in the EU.
17113.m: Germany is the most populous country in the EU.

17114.q: Which is the smallest country in the European Union by area?
17114.e: Malta is an island state in the Mediterranean and only about 316 km² in size. Luxembourg, at around 2,600 km², is much bigger.
17114.m: Malta is the smallest country in the EU.

17115.q: What is the capital of Portugal?
17115.e: Lisbon lies where the Tagus flows into the Atlantic. Porto is the second largest city in Portugal.
17115.m: The capital of Portugal is Lisbon.

17116.q: What is the capital of Poland?
17116.e: Warsaw lies on the Vistula and is the largest city in Poland. Kraków was a royal city for a long time.
17116.m: The capital of Poland is Warsaw.

17117.q: What is the capital of Croatia?
17117.e: Zagreb lies inland in the north of Croatia. Split and Dubrovnik are well-known cities on the Adriatic coast.
17117.m: The capital of Croatia is Zagreb.

17118.q: Officially, Switzerland has no capital. What is Bern called instead?
17118.e: The Federal Council and the Federal Assembly have their seat in Bern. But the Federal Constitution names no capital, so people speak of the federal city.

17119.q: Which has been the largest country in Africa by area since 2011?
17119.e: When South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011, Algeria, at around 2.4 million km², became the largest country in Africa. Much of it is desert.
17119.m: Algeria is the largest country in Africa.

17120.q: Which country in Africa has the most inhabitants?
17120.e: Nigeria in West Africa has over 200 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That means about one in six people in Africa lives there.
17120.m: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa.

17121.q: Which country is Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, in?
17121.e: Kilimanjaro is about 5,895 m high and lies in north-eastern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya. Its highest peak is the volcano Kibo, which has been dormant for a long time.

17122.q: Which country is completely surrounded by the territory of South Africa?
17122.e: Lesotho is an enclave and lies entirely inside South Africa. It is a mountainous country with high valleys.
17122.m: Lesotho lies in the middle of South Africa.

17123.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17123.e: Tokyo lies on the main island of Honshu. Kyoto was the imperial city for over 1,000 years.
17123.m: The capital of Japan is Tokyo.

17124.q: Which country lies entirely in Asia and is the largest by area?
17124.e: China is about 9.6 million km² in size. Russia is bigger, but part of it lies in Europe.
17124.m: China is the largest country that lies entirely in Asia.

17125.q: Which island state in South-East Asia is made up of around 17,000 islands?
17125.e: Indonesia is the largest island state in the world. Among the best-known islands are Java, Bali and Sumatra.
17125.m: Indonesia is the largest island state on Earth.

18192.q: Which instrument measures how warm or cold it is?
18192.e: A thermometer shows the temperature. You read it in degrees Celsius.

18193.q: What is the forecast called that tells you what the weather will be like tomorrow?
18193.e: In the weather forecast, experts say what the weather will be like over the next few days. You find it on the radio, on TV or on the internet.
18193.m: The weather forecast tells you the weather in advance.

18194.q: What are the little drops of water on the grass early in the morning called?
18194.e: During the cool night, water forms from the damp air. In the morning, little drops sparkle on the grass.
18194.m: Dew is little drops of water in the morning.

18195.q: What do you call a cloud that lies right down on the ground?
18195.e: Fog is a cloud that lies right down on the ground. Then you cannot see very far.
18195.m: Fog is a cloud on the ground.

18196.q: What are the small balls of ice that fall from the sky in a storm called?
18196.e: Hailstones are balls of ice. They form in big thunderclouds.
18196.m: Hail is made of small balls of ice.

18197.q: In which direction does the sun set in the evening?
18197.e: In the evening the sun disappears in the west. After that it gets dark.
18197.m: The sun sets in the west.

18198.q: What protects your skin from sunburn in summer?
18198.e: Sun cream blocks some of the strong rays of the sun. A hat and clothes protect you too.
18198.m: Sun cream protects your skin from sunburn.

18199.q: Why must you never look straight at the sun?
18199.e: Bright sunlight can injure your eyes. That is why you never look straight at it.
18199.m: Looking straight at the sun harms your eyes.

18200.q: Apart from light, what does the sun give us?
18200.e: The sun sends light and warmth to the Earth. Without it, the Earth would be freezing cold.
18200.m: The sun gives us light and warmth.

18201.q: What is a raindrop made of?
18201.e: A raindrop is a little drop of water. Lots of drops together are rain.

18202.q: What is often left on paths and roads after it rains?
18202.e: The rainwater collects in little dips. That is how puddles form.

18203.q: What do plants need rain for?
18203.e: Plants need water to grow. The rain brings them this water.

18204.q: Which animal often comes out of the ground after it rains?
18204.e: After rain, earthworms often crawl up to the surface. You can see them on paths and meadows.
18204.m: Lots of earthworms come out after rain.

18205.q: What do you take with you to keep your head dry in the rain?
18205.e: An umbrella keeps off the drops from above. That way you stay dry.
18205.m: An umbrella keeps the rain off.

18206.q: How many points does a snowflake usually have?
18206.e: Snow crystals usually have six points or sides. Even so, every flake looks a little different.
18206.m: A snowflake usually has six points.

18207.q: What happens to snow when it gets warm?
18207.e: When it is warm, snow melts. The snow turns into water.
18207.m: Snow melts into water when it is warm.

18208.q: What can you build out of snow?
18208.e: With wet snow you can roll balls. You use them to build a snowman.
18208.m: You can build a snowman out of snow.

18209.q: What do you call a large amount of snow that slides down a mountain?
18209.e: An avalanche is snow that slides quickly down a slope. Avalanches are dangerous.
18209.m: An avalanche is snow sliding down a mountain.

18210.e: Wind is air that moves. You cannot see it, but you can feel it.

18211.q: Which toy do you fly in the wind in autumn?
18211.e: A kite is lifted into the air by the wind. In autumn it is often windy.
18211.m: A kite flies with the wind.

18212.q: What is a very strong wind that can blow trees over called?
18212.e: A storm is a very strong wind. It can blow trees over and damage roofs.
18212.m: A storm is a very strong wind.

18213.q: What turns on a wind turbine when the wind blows?
18213.e: The wind turns the blades of the wind turbine. This makes electricity.
18213.m: The wind turns the blades of a wind turbine.

18214.q: What is the warm wind called that blows down into the valleys of the Swiss Alps?
18214.e: The föhn is a warm, dry wind. In Switzerland it blows, for example, in the canton of Uri and in the Rhine valley.
18214.m: The föhn is a warm wind in the Alps.

18215.q: What is the cold wind called that often blows from the north-east in Switzerland?
18215.e: The bise is a cold, dry wind from the north-east. It often blows across the Swiss Plateau.
18215.m: The bise is a cold wind from the north-east.

18216.e: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They float in the air.
18216.m: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets.

18217.q: What colour are clouds often before it rains heavily?
18217.e: Thick rain clouds let little light through. That is why they look dark grey.

18218.q: What do fleecy “sheep” clouds look like?
a: Like little balls of cotton wool
18218.e: Fleecy clouds are lots of small white clouds. They look like a flock of sheep.
18218.m: Fleecy clouds look like little balls of cotton wool.

18219.q: What do you see flash in the sky during a thunderstorm?
18219.e: Lightning is a bright electric spark in the air. It only flashes for a very short time.

18220.q: What is the loud crash after a flash of lightning called?
18220.e: Lightning heats the air very strongly. This makes a loud bang: the thunder.
18220.m: After the lightning comes the thunder.

18221.q: In a thunderstorm, what reaches you first?
18221.e: Light is much faster than sound. That is why you see the lightning before you hear the thunder.
18221.m: You see the lightning before the thunder.

18222.q: Where are you safest during a thunderstorm?
18222.e: In a house or a car you are protected from lightning. Trees, hills and water are dangerous.
18222.m: In a thunderstorm, go into a house.

18223.q: In which season are there the most thunderstorms in Switzerland?
18223.e: In summer the air is warm and damp. Thunderstorms often form from it.

18224.q: What protects a house from being struck by lightning?
18224.e: A lightning conductor carries the lightning safely into the ground. That way the house is not damaged.
18224.m: A lightning conductor protects the house from lightning.

18225.q: What is needed for a rainbow to appear?
18225.e: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines on raindrops. The drops split the light into colours.
18225.m: For a rainbow you need sun and rain.

18226.q: Which colour is on the very outside of a rainbow?
18226.e: In a rainbow, red is on the outside. Violet is right on the inside.
18226.m: In a rainbow, red is on the very outside.

18227.e: A rainbow is a coloured arch in the sky. From an aeroplane you can sometimes see a whole circle.
18227.m: A rainbow is shaped like an arch.

18228.q: Where must the sun be when you see a rainbow?
18228.e: You only see a rainbow with the sun behind you. The rain is then in front of you.
18228.m: You see a rainbow with the sun behind you.

18229.q: Which colour is NOT in a rainbow?
18229.e: A rainbow has red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Brown is not one of them.
18229.m: Brown is not in a rainbow.

18230.q: In which season do the leaves fall from many trees?
18230.e: In autumn the leaves turn colourful and fall off. This helps the trees save water in winter.

18231.q: In which season do the first flowers such as snowdrops bloom?
18231.e: In spring it gets warmer. Then the first flowers bloom.
18231.m: The first flowers bloom in spring.

18232.q: In which season are the days longest?
18232.e: In summer the sun shines for the longest time. That is why it stays light late in the evening.
18232.m: The days are longest in summer.

18233.e: The order is spring, summer, autumn, winter. After winter comes spring again.

18234.q: What is the highest point of a mountain called?
18234.e: The summit is the highest place on a mountain. There is often a summit cross there.
18234.m: The summit is the highest point of a mountain.

18235.q: What is the big mountain range in Switzerland with very high mountains called?
18235.e: The Alps are the highest mountains in Switzerland. They cover more than half of the country.
18235.m: The Alps are the highest mountains in Switzerland.

18236.q: Which Swiss mountain is famous for its pointed shape?
18236.e: The Matterhorn near Zermatt has a very pointed shape. It is one of the best-known mountains in the world.
18236.m: The Matterhorn is famous for its pointed shape.

18237.q: What are the mountains in the north-west of Switzerland called?
18237.e: The Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland. Its mountains are lower than the Alps.
18237.m: The Jura is in the north-west of Switzerland.

18238.q: How does the temperature usually change when you climb a high mountain?
18238.e: The higher you climb, the colder the air gets. That is why there is often snow on high mountains.
18238.m: The higher you climb, the colder it gets.

18239.e: A valley is lower land between mountains. A river often flows along the bottom.
18239.m: A valley lies low between mountains.

18240.q: What often flows along the bottom of a valley?
18240.e: A river flows through many valleys. The water often helped to shape the valley itself.
18240.m: A river flows through many valleys.

18241.q: Which letter shape does a valley carved out by a glacier have?
18241.e: A glacier grinds the valley out wide. That is why it is shaped like a U.
18241.m: A glacier valley is shaped like a U.

18242.q: Which letter shape does a valley dug by a river have?
18242.e: A river digs deep and narrow into the ground. That is why the valley looks like a V.
18242.m: A river valley is shaped like a V.

18243.q: Which big river flows through Valais?
18243.e: The Rhône flows through the main valley of Valais. Then it flows into Lake Geneva.

18244.q: What is the place where a river begins called?
18244.e: At the source, water comes out of the ground. That is where a stream or river begins.
18244.m: A river begins at its source.

18245.q: What is the place called where a river flows into another river, a lake or the sea?
18245.e: The mouth is the end of a river. There it flows into another body of water.
18245.m: A river ends at its mouth.

18246.q: Which big river flows through Basel?
18246.e: The Rhine flows through Basel and on to the North Sea. Basel has an important Rhine port.

18247.q: What do you call a small river?
18247.e: A stream is a small, narrow flowing water. Several streams together can form a river.
18247.m: A small river is called a stream.

18248.q: What is the edge of a river called?
18248.e: The bank is the land right next to the water. You can go for a walk there.
18248.m: The edge of a river is called the bank.

18249.e: A lake is still water in the middle of the land. All around it is land.
18249.m: A lake is water surrounded by land.

18250.q: Which is the largest lake in Switzerland?
18250.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland. Part of it belongs to France.
18250.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.

18251.q: Which big lake lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria?
18251.e: Lake Constance lies in the north-east of Switzerland. Three countries border it.

18252.q: What is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland?
18252.e: Lake Neuchâtel lies completely in Switzerland. We share Lake Geneva and Lake Constance with other countries.
18252.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely in Switzerland.

18253.q: What is a small, often shallow body of still water called?
18253.e: A pond is a small body of still water. Frogs and dragonflies often live there.
18253.m: A pond is a small body of water.

18254.q: Is the water in Swiss lakes salty or fresh?
18254.e: Swiss lakes have fresh water. The water in the sea is salty.

18255.q: What is a glacier made of?
18255.e: A glacier is a huge mass of ice. It forms from snow that is pressed together over many years.
18255.m: A glacier is made of ice.

18256.q: What is the longest glacier in the Alps called?
18256.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the longest glacier in the Alps. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
18256.m: The Aletsch Glacier is the longest glacier in the Alps.

a: Yes, as fast as a car
18257.e: A glacier flows very slowly down the valley. You cannot see the movement with your eyes.

18258.q: What is happening to most glaciers in Switzerland at the moment?
18258.e: Because it is getting warmer, the glaciers are melting. Many have shrunk a lot in recent years.

18259.q: What are deep cracks in glacier ice called?
18259.e: Crevasses are deep cracks in the ice. They are very dangerous, so people only cross them roped together.
18259.m: Crevasses are deep cracks in the ice.

18260.q: What is the hot, liquid rock that flows out of a volcano called?
18260.e: Lava is melted rock from deep inside the Earth. It is about 800 to 1200 degrees hot.
18260.m: Lava is liquid rock from a volcano.

18261.q: What is the opening at the top of a volcano called?
18261.e: The crater is the hole at the top of the volcano. Lava and ash come out of it during an eruption.
18261.m: The crater is at the top of the volcano.

18262.q: What do you call it when a volcano throws out lava and ash?
18262.e: In an eruption, lava, ash and gases come out of the volcano. That can be very dangerous.

18263.q: Are there active volcanoes in Switzerland today?
18263.e: There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland today. Active volcanoes in Europe can be found, for example, in Italy and Iceland.
18263.m: There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland.

18264.q: Which famous volcano is on the Italian island of Sicily?
18264.e: Etna is on Sicily. It is one of the most active volcanoes in Europe.

18265.e: In an earthquake the Earth moves and the ground shakes. Strong earthquakes can damage houses.
18265.m: In an earthquake the ground shakes.

18266.q: Where is the best place to hide in a house during an earthquake?
18266.e: Under a sturdy table you are protected from things falling down. Windows and lifts are dangerous.
18266.m: In an earthquake, protect yourself under a sturdy table.

18267.q: In which canton is the risk of earthquakes highest in Switzerland?
18267.e: Valais has the highest earthquake risk in Switzerland. But most earthquakes there are so weak that you cannot feel them.
18267.m: Valais has the highest earthquake risk.

18268.q: Can you feel most earthquakes in Switzerland?
18268.e: There are many earthquakes in Switzerland every year. But most are so weak that only measuring instruments notice them.
18268.m: Most earthquakes are too weak to feel.

18269.q: Which present-day Swiss city was destroyed by a strong earthquake in 1356?
18269.e: The Basel earthquake of 1356 is the strongest known earthquake in Central Europe. Large parts of the city were destroyed.
18269.m: Basel was destroyed by an earthquake in 1356.

18270.q: At how many degrees Celsius does water freeze?
18270.e: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. Below that it stays solid.

18271.q: At how many degrees Celsius does water boil?
18271.e: Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius. Then it turns into steam.
18271.m: Water boils at a hundred degrees.

18272.q: Why is Switzerland often called the “water tower of Europe”?
18272.e: Big rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône start in the Swiss Alps. They flow into many countries in Europe.
18272.m: Switzerland is called the water tower of Europe.

18273.q: What covers most of the Earth’s surface?
18273.e: More than two thirds of the Earth’s surface is covered with water. Most of it is sea water.
18273.m: Most of the Earth is covered with water.

18274.q: Does ice float in water or sink?
18274.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why it floats on top, like ice cubes in a glass.

18275.q: What are the pointed sticks of ice that hang from the roof in winter called?
18275.e: When water drips from the roof and freezes, icicles grow. They hang downwards.
18275.m: Icicles hang from the roof in winter.

18276.q: What is a huge chunk of ice floating in the sea called?
18276.e: An iceberg is a big chunk of ice in the sea. Most of it is hidden under the water.
18276.m: Most of an iceberg is under the water.

18277.q: What is dangerous on a frozen lake?
18277.e: Thin ice can break. Only go onto the ice when grown-ups have said it is allowed.

18278.q: What is spread on roads in winter to make the ice melt?
18278.e: Salt makes ice melt even when it is cold. That is why municipalities spread salt on the roads in winter.
18278.m: Salt makes ice on the road melt.

18279.q: What happens when the sun warms the water in the sea?
18279.e: The sun warms the water. Some of it rises into the air as invisible water vapour.

18280.q: What forms when water vapour cools high up?
18280.e: High up in the air it is cold. The cooled vapour gathers there and clouds form.

18281.q: How does the water from the clouds get back down to Earth?
18281.e: The water falls to Earth as rain, snow or hail. Experts call this precipitation.
18281.m: Rain or snow falls from clouds.

18282.q: Where does the rainwater in streams and rivers flow in the end?
18282.e: Streams and rivers carry the water back to the sea. There the cycle starts all over again.
18282.m: Rivers carry the water back to the sea.

18283.q: Why doesn’t the Earth run out of water?
a: It moves round in a cycle
18283.e: Water evaporates, forms clouds, rains down and flows back to the sea. It is used again and again.
18283.m: Water moves round in a cycle.

18284.q: What is the water called that soaks into the ground and collects under the earth?
18284.e: Some of the rain soaks into the ground and collects as groundwater. In Switzerland, a large part of the drinking water comes from groundwater.

18285.q: Into how many main layers is the Earth divided according to its chemical make-up?
18285.e: We distinguish the crust, the mantle and the core. These layers differ in their materials and their density.
18285.m: The Earth is made up of crust, mantle and core.

18286.q: Which layer makes up most of the Earth’s volume?
